column4: The section gives burial as a dictionary sense of 93:7’s ض ل ل root; here the speakers ask whether, after being lost into earth, they will be in a new creation. It is the Quranic objection that makes burial the question of renewed existence.

The section identifies 93:4’s al-ākhirah word with second creation; in God’s answer within Moses’ account, people are made from earth, returned to it, then brought out another time (أُخْرَىٰ). This completes the transition disputed in 32:10.

The verse after 32:10 says the appointed Angel of Death takes people and they are returned to their Lord. It contributes the death-and-return sequence that the preceding question about becoming a new creation leaves unresolved.

The section quotes this verse’s “place of settlement” and “place of deposit” (مُسْتَقَرٌّ وَمُسْتَوْدَعٌ) as spanning the passage between being entrusted and remaining; the verse itself locates both in human creation from one soul.
The section moves from a corpse covered and buried toward new existence; this verse states that God causes a human to die and gives him burial, naming the funeral act directly.
After death and burial in 80:21, this verse says that when God wills, He raises the person (أَنشَرَهُ). It supplies the image’s movement from burial to renewed life.
After killing his brother, one son of Adam sees a crow scratch the earth and learn how to bury the corpse. This is the section’s burial image enacted as a scene.
God says people will live on earth, die there, and be brought out from it; the verse states the soil-to-life passage that the section’s burial and renewed-being image carries.
The disbelievers ask whether, after dying and becoming dust, they will return; this repeats the section’s burial-to-new-creation question, alongside the burial sense of 93:7’s ض ل ل root.

The answer to the dust objection in 50:3 says God knows what the earth diminishes from bodies and has a preserving record. It adds that bodily loss into earth does not erase the person from divine knowledge.

The section notes that the orphan named in 93:6 stands behind a dead father; here two orphan boys’ righteous father is explicitly recalled, and their hidden treasure is kept for them until maturity. The father’s death is presupposed by their orphan status rather than narrated.
At death, a person asks to be sent back so he can act rightly; this gives the funeral transition a human voice at the moment life ends.
The answer to the request in 23:99 places a barrier behind the dead until the day they are raised. It marks the boundary between burial and the later return the section evokes.
The verse says God returns people to the earth and then brings them out from it; it gives the clearest parallel to burial followed by emergence.
At the trumpet, people come out of their graves and hasten to their Lord. The grave opening is the scene that carries the section’s move from burial to renewed existence.
Those raised in 36:51 ask who woke them from their resting place; the verse answers that this is what the Merciful promised. Its contribution is the dead person’s own recognition of resurrection.
The verse says graves will be overturned; it directly stages the opening of burial places at the transition to judgment.
The earth is shaken with its final shaking; 99:2 supplies the next verse’s detail that it casts out its burdens. This row contributes the upheaval that opens the burial scene.
The earth casts out its burdens after the shaking in 99:1, a direct image of what was held within the ground coming out.
The verse asks whether people know that what is in the graves will be scattered out. It names the buried contents that the section’s burial image leaves under the earth.
The verse joins the coming Hour to God’s raising those in the graves, making the funeral ground the place from which the next life begins.
People emerge from the graves hurriedly on the day they are summoned; this is a direct Quranic scene of burial ending in rising.
The verse depicts people coming out of graves with humbled eyes, dispersed like locusts. The grave-opening scene directly parallels the section’s passage from burial to life again.
The deniers ask whether bones and fragments can be raised as a new creation. It is the same objection to renewed being after bodily decomposition that the section cites in 32:10.
The deniers ask if bones and dust will be raised as a new creation; this repeats the section’s central dispute with the corpse reduced to earth.
The objection asks whether becoming dust is followed by a new creation. It restates the section’s precise passage from burial to renewed existence.
The people ask whether, after dying and becoming dust and bones, they will be brought out; the verse directly disputes the same post-burial emergence.
The speakers ask whether people will be raised after death, dust, and bones. This is another direct version of the section’s burial-to-new-creation question.
The deniers ask whether people will be raised after death, dust, and bones; the bodily stages match the section’s movement from burial toward another existence.
A companion is asked whether, after death and becoming dust and bones, he will be judged; the question again places bodily decay against life after death.
The deniers ask whether they will be raised after dying and becoming dust and bones, directly repeating the image’s central objection.
The deniers ask whether they will be returned to their former state; 79:11 specifies the decayed bones they mean. This row contributes their question about return after death.
The next part of the question in 79:10 asks whether they will return when they have become decayed bones; it makes bodily dissolution the obstacle to renewed life.
They call the return in 79:10–11 a ruinous return. This verse gives the resistance to the same resurrection the section traces from burial to new existence.
The answer says there will be only one blast; 79:14 gives its immediate result. It supplies the decisive act that ends the deniers’ imagined impossibility of return.
After the single blast in 79:13, people are suddenly awake on the earth’s surface. It completes the passage from the bones imagined below ground to life above it.
The challenger asks who can give life to bones after they have crumbled; this makes the decomposed body itself the test of renewed existence.
The answer to the broken-bone challenge in 36:78 is that the One who made them the first time will revive them. It links the first making to the life that follows bodily decay.
The verse asks whether the human thinks God will not gather his bones; it makes bodily reassembly the concrete question after death.
The answer in the next verse says God can restore even the fingertips; it adds precise reconstruction to the gathering of bones in 75:3.
When God calls people from the earth, they come forth; this is a concise scene of emergence from the ground that completes the section’s burial-to-life movement.
The verse says God caused people to grow from the earth like plants; it connects human existence to the same earth from which the section says the buried are brought back.
The verse moves from human creation from dust to the revival of dead earth, then uses that sign in its address about resurrection. It connects earth as origin, burial-place, and renewed life.
God sends water and revives a dead land, then says people will likewise be brought out. The verse makes the earth’s return to life an explicit counterpart to resurrection.
After describing dead land made alive by rain, the verse says resurrection is likewise; it supplies an earth-based analogy for life after death.
God revives the earth after its death, and the verse asks whether the One who did so can give life to the dead. It explicitly bridges the dead ground to the dead person.
Rain revives dead land, and the verse compares this to bringing the dead forth. It gives the same earth-to-life pattern as the section’s burial image.
The verse turns living into dead and dead into living, revives earth after its death, and says people will be brought out; it gathers the section’s two movements in one formulation.
The section reads 93:4’s al-ākhirah-root word through second creation; this verse explicitly names the other creation (النَّشْأَةَ الْأُخْرَىٰ), directly matching renewed existence.
The deniers ask whether, after being torn apart, they will be in a new creation. The verse directly contests the same possibility of life after bodily dissolution.
The deniers swear that God will not raise the dead; 16:39 answers that He will raise them to make clear what they disputed. This row states the denial answered by the section’s resurrection arc.
The speakers say that they only die and live in worldly life and will not be raised. This directly rejects the passage from death to a later existence.
The deniers say there is only worldly life, with people dying and living while time destroys them; this is the contrary boundary to the section’s movement into life after death.
The deniers say they will not be raised, and the reply swears that they will be. This is an explicit boundary between denial of resurrection and the section’s renewed-being image.
The verse describes people as dead, then given life, then made to die and live again before returning to God; it sets out the existence-death-return sequence behind the section’s image.
The speakers acknowledge two deaths and two lives before confessing their sins; this is a compact formulation of death followed by renewed existence.
God creates, provides, causes death, and gives life again; this explicit sequence matches the section’s movement from existence through death to life.
God gives life and causes death, and to Him people return; it states the passage from mortality to return that underlies the image.
The verse asks whether people have seen God begin creation and then repeat it; this is the section’s second-creation claim stated as a direct question.
The next verse directs people to observe how creation began and says God will bring about the latter creation; it completes the first-making/re-creation claim in 29:19.
God originates creation and repeats it, then people are returned to Him; this directly matches the section’s second existence.
The verse says God originates creation and repeats it, and that repeating it is easy for Him; it gives the section’s renewed-creation claim in another direct formulation.
The verse asks who begins creation and then repeats it; the repeated making is the exact idea the section hears in its al-ākhirah word.
The verse states that God originates and repeats creation, directly echoing the section’s passage from not-being to being again.
The section’s dictionary form for the root و ج د describes a thing coming into existence after nonexistence; this verse asks whether the human remembers being created when previously nothing.
The section’s dictionary form for و ج د describes existence after nonexistence; this verse asks whether people were created from nothing or created themselves, making the origin question explicit.
The section’s dictionary form for و ج د names coming to exist after not existing; this verse asks whether a time passed when the human was not even a thing mentioned.
The verse places the final and the first with God; it echoes the al-ākhirah/al-ūlā pair named in the section and the passage from first life to what follows.
The verse says the first and the hereafter belong to God; its surah also opens with night covering and day appearing, so it brings together the section’s night-covering and first/afterlife word-pair.
The verse says that if God wills He can remove people and bring a new creation; it extends the section’s new-being theme from an individual burial to replacement of a whole people.
This verse says such replacement is not difficult for God, completing the new-creation claim in 14:19.
The verse says God causes death and life; it gives the section’s death-to-life movement in a compressed form without its burial scene.
God gives life and death and gathers people for the Day, while the verse records that many do not know this; it makes the section’s life-beyond-death boundary explicit.
God decrees death among people and says no one can escape or be prevented; it makes the funeral image’s mortality a divine limit.
The verse says God can replace people and create them in a form they do not know; it completes the death decree in 56:60 with renewed creation.
The verse recalls the first creation and asks why people do not remember; it supplies first-making as evidence for the second creation in the preceding two ayat.
After describing human formation earlier, this verse says people will surely die; 23:16 gives the separate contribution of being raised on the Day of Resurrection.
The verse says people will be raised on the Day of Resurrection after the death stated in 23:15, completing the life-to-death-to-life sequence.
When death comes, God’s messengers take the person and he is returned to God, his true Master; it gives the passage from bodily death to return without naming the grave.
God takes people at night, then raises them by day and returns them to life until their appointed term; this links the section’s literal night scene to a reversible passage resembling death.

God takes souls at death and during sleep, retaining those for whom death is decreed and releasing the others. It links night’s withdrawal to death while preserving the boundary between sleep and final death.
The verse says people choose the nearer life; it supplies the contrast to the section’s 93:4 movement from the first life toward the hereafter.
The verse says the hereafter is better and more lasting; it makes explicit the lasting side of the passage from this life toward what follows.
The verse contrasts what passes away with what remains with God; it makes mortality and lasting existence perceptible in the section’s move from burial to renewed life.
God creates death and life to test people; the verse presents death as part of a purposeful passage rather than an end, matching the section’s movement beyond burial.
The source section’s dictionary gloss for 93:2’s sajā includes a cloth spread over the dead; here night itself covers, so the covering scene echoes that gloss, while this ayah speaks of night.

The source section’s dictionary gloss for 93:2’s sajā includes a burial covering; this verse pictures night covering the day/sun. The connection is only the covering scene, not a claim that the verse depicts death.

The source section’s dictionary gloss for 93:2 describes cloth covering a corpse; here the addressee is “the wrapped one” (الْمُدَّثِّرُ), a living person, so the shared covering becomes a clear reversal of the shroud scene.

After addressing the living “wrapped one” in 74:1, this verse commands him to rise and warn; it adds movement and proclamation after covering, in contrast to the corpse in the section’s dictionary gloss.

The source section’s dictionary gloss for 93:2 connects covering to a dead body; this verse addresses a living person wrapped in garments at night. The parallel is the covered figure, with the difference in life status explicit.
The command to stand at night follows the wrapped figure in 73:1; it completes that living, nocturnal scene and contrasts with the burial covering in the section’s dictionary gloss.

The section identifies the root of 93:11’s “tell” with the dictionary form الحدوث, coming into being after not-being; this verse uses a related form for a newly arriving reminder. Its context is new revelation, not bodily resurrection, so the link is lexical and limited.

The verse says the living and dead are not alike and that a messenger cannot make those in graves hear. It marks a boundary between the section’s death vocabulary and its later language of being and telling.
The verse says the dead cannot hear a call; it marks the limit of communication across burial, a counterpoint to the section’s movement from death-associated words toward telling.
The verse says the dead cannot be made to hear; it gives the same explicit limit on speech across graves that bounds the section’s lexical movement toward narration.

The verse forbids calling those killed in God’s way dead, saying they are alive with their Lord; it reverses the funeral status in the section and marks a boundary between bodily death and continued life.
